entries.title: Can UN chief's initiative kickstart resolution for Cyprus?
entries.summary: UN chief Antonio Guterres considers a resolution to the Cyprus issue to be vital for regional stability and has initiated a new diplomatic effort. What are the prospects for its success?
entries.content:
Cyprus

Can UN chief's initiative kickstart resolution for Cyprus?

August 6, 2026

UN chief Antonio Guterres considers a resolution to the Cyprus issue to be vital for regional stability and has initiated a new diplomatic effort. What are the prospects for its success?

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres last week became the first UN chief to visit Cyprus in 16 years.

While there, he met the leaders of the island's two communities: Nikos Christodoulides, president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Tufan Erhurman, Turkish Cypriot leader and president of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is only recognized by Turkey.

His aim in doing so was to determine whether the conditions exist for restarting negotiations on the Cyprus issue.

Progress on talks has remained stalled since the collapse of negotiations in Crans-Montana, Switzerland, in 2017, when the United Nations made its most comprehensive effort to broker a reunification agreement for the island.

Why now?

So, why has Antonio Guterres decided to launch a new initiative now?

According to diplomatic sources, the answer lies less in developments surrounding the Cyprus issue itself and more in the rapidly changing geopolitical landscape of the wider region.

War in the Middle East, deteriorating relations between Israel and Turkey, and growing strategic competition in the Eastern Mediterranean have heightened UN concerns that the unresolved Cyprus conflict could undermine the stability of the entire region.

Guterres said as much after the joint meeting on July 29. "I do believe that a solution in Cyprus is absolutely crucial, not only to preserve the interests and the peace of the Cyprus people, but also as a factor of stability in what is becoming a dangerously unstable region," he said.

Speaking to DW, Andreas Mavroyiannis, former permanent representative of the Republic of Cyprus to the United Nations and former chief negotiator of the Greek Cypriot side, shared the same concern.

"The strengthening of relations between the Republic of Cyprus and Israel, combined with the deterioration of Israel–Turkey relations, increases the risk of the Cyprus issue being instrumentalized," he told DW.

According to Mavroyiannis, the UN secretary-general fears that Cyprus could, instead of serving as a pillar of stability in the Middle East, become increasingly entangled in regional rivalries and emerge as one of the area's most vulnerable flashpoints.

The European dimension

The UN is not alone in viewing the Cyprus issue through the prism of regional security. The EU has also shown increasing interest in playing a more active political role in efforts to revive the peace process.

A significant step came on July 7, when the European Commission appointed Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto as the EU's Special Representative for the Cyprus issue.

His mandate is to support the UN-led process and strengthen the bloc's involvement in efforts to restart negotiations.

A more active role for the EU has long been one of President Nikos Christodoulides' key policy objectives.

During Cyprus' recent presidency of the Council of the European Union, he reminded fellow European leaders that he was "the president of the only EU member state that remains under illegal military occupation."

The Cypriot government believes that the EU agenda could provide Ankara with incentives to contribute constructively to progress on the Cyprus issue.

Among the issues viewed as potential leverage are the modernization of the EU–Turkey Customs Union, visa liberalization for Turkish citizens, Turkey's participation in the EU's SAFE defense financing instrument and the prospect of gradually reviving its long-frozen EU accession process.

The next step

While Guterres' decision to announce a new informal expanded 5+1 meeting involving the two Cypriot communities, the three guarantor powers (Greece, Turkey and the UK) plus the UN was widely seen as a positive signal, he deliberately stopped short of setting a date.

Instead, he made it clear that the meeting would only be convened once sufficient progress had been made on confidence-building measures, methodology and the substance of the process.

So, it was no coincidence that he stressed upon arriving in Cyprus that "it depends obviously on the Cypriots themselves," underlining that responsibility for moving the process forward rests primarily with the two communities.

His remarks are directly linked to the lack of tangible progress on confidence-building measures.

Despite months of discussions, the two sides failed to reach agreement even on the opening of new crossing points — a step which, according to the UN Secretary-General, could have "a tangible impact on the daily lives of Cypriots," while helping to restore a minimum level of trust ahead of the next phase of negotiations.

Ankara's position remains crucial

The key question, however, extends beyond the two communities themselves and concerns Turkey's willingness to engage.

The real test for the UN is whether Ankara is prepared to return to negotiations conducted within the framework of the UN Security Council resolutions and the agreed basis of a bicommunal, bizonal federation, moving away from the two-state solution it has advocated since the collapse of the Crans-Montana talks in 2017.

So far, Turkey has made no public statement indicating such a shift. The only possible indication comes indirectly from Antonio Guterres' remark that he has "the consent of both sides and the guarantor powers to move towards another 5+1 meeting, provided there is adequate preparation."

The wording suggests that, at least procedurally, Ankara is willing to participate in another informal conference under UN auspices. Whether this also signals a substantive change in Turkey's long-standing position remains, for now, an open question.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: Why Iran is sending mixed signals on talks
entries.summary: Trump says talks with Iran are underway. Tehran says it is discussing the Strait of Hormuz with Oman, not Washington. Analysts say the gap reflects competing political pressures.
entries.content:
Iran

Why Iran is sending mixed signals on talks

August 6, 2026

Trump says talks with Iran are underway. Tehran says it is discussing the Strait of Hormuz with Oman, not Washington. Analysts say the gap reflects competing political pressures.

US President Donald Trump on Monday said that negotiations with Iran were ongoing over the Strait of Hormuz, adding that the Islamic Republic was facing a "last chance before decapitation." 

Trump told reporters at the White House that he agreed to continue to pursue talks with Iran at the request of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other countries.

His remarks appeared to contradict public statements from Tehran, which has so far denied that negotiations with Washington were taking place.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei nevertheless confirmed that Tehran was holding talks with Oman over the strategic waterway. 

The two sides may therefore be describing the same diplomatic channel in different terms, each using language aimed at its own domestic audience.

Washington describes the Omani mediation as negotiations with Iran. Tehran portrays it as a technical discussion with Oman about shipping through the strait.

Hormuz remains the main obstacle

The Strait of Hormuz has become the main sticking point.

Commercial traffic through key waterway remains severely restricted, while ships continue to face attacks near the strait.

According to data from maritime analytics company Kpler cited by Reuters news agency, only six commercial vessels crossed the route on Monday, down from seven the previous day.

The uncertainty surrounding the key waterway has also affected global markets.

Hopes of diplomatic progress recently pushed oil prices lower and helped stock markets rise. But those movements reflected how sensitive markets remain to any news about the strait, rather than evidence that the crisis had been resolved.

Iran wants some measure of control over vessels entering the Persian Gulf to be recognized. The United States wants the strait fully reopened to unrestricted international shipping.

Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW that the disagreement is no longer simply about whether the two sides are talking.

"The question is what to call those talks and what each side hopes to gain from them," he said.

Trump describes the indirect channel as negotiations because he needs to show that military and economic pressure has brought Tehran back to the table, Dorbeiki said.

He suggested that Iran avoids the same terminology because acknowledging negotiations with Washington could be seen by its domestic opponents as surrender.

The two sides remain far apart.

"Iran wants control over vessels entering the strait, while the United States wants completely free passage," Dorbeiki said. "These positions cannot easily be reconciled."

Divisions inside Iran

The contradictory messages also reflect divisions between rival political factions inside Iran.

Dorbeiki identifies two broad camps.

"The first, which could be described as the 'development and reconstruction through agreement' camp, believes that without sanctions relief and the reopening of Hormuz, Iran's economy cannot recover or even sustain itself," he told DW.

According to Dorbeiki, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and some Revolutionary Guard figures with economic interests may be closer to that view.

The opposing camp, which includes the Paydari Front, a small, ultra-conservative party, "sees an agreement with the United States as an ideological defeat" and favors continued resistance.

Leadership vacuum adds to uncertainty

The lack of a clear leader in Iran has added to the uncertainty.

Since the country's then supreme leader Ali Khamenei was killed in an airstrike on February 28 the first hours of the US-Israeli war against Iran, authority has become more fragmented.

His son Mojtaba Khamenei was named new supreme leader, but his role remains unclear and he has not been seen in public since the war began amid speculation he was severely injured in the strike.

Dorbeiki says this has allowed rival groups to claim they speak for the leadership.

"Indirect talks through Oman are likely to continue," he told DW. "Pezeshkian will remain under pressure, but he is unlikely to be removed for now because the domestic and international political costs would be high."

Dorbeiki noted that keeping Pezeshkian in office leaves open the option of blaming him if the negotiations fail.

Three competing camps inside Iran

Hassan Asadi Zeidabadi, an Iranian political analyst based in Tehran, believes the main decision-makers in Tehran have already accepted the need for negotiations.

However, he says there are three main camps within the Iranian establishment.

The first consists of government officials dealing with the economic effects of the war and blockade, making them more inclined toward negotiations.

"The second group is made up mainly of military figures who want to improve their position in the conflict before negotiating and remain skeptical of US intentions," Zeidabadi told DW.

"The third group is made up of ideological hardliners who believe that reaching an agreement with Washington after the war and the killing of Iran's supreme leader would mark the end of the Islamic Republic's traditional identity, which is rooted in opposition to the West."

"They fear the day after an agreement," Asadi Zeidabadi added. "For them, a deal with the United States would mean the end of the ideological era they represent and, ultimately, their own removal."

Zeidabadi said these hardliners retain influence in parliament, the security establishment and the state's propaganda apparatus, and fear the changes a deal could bring.

The future of the talks may depend less on Muscat or Washington than on which factions gain the upper hand in Tehran.

If supporters of an agreement convince the leadership that continued isolation threatens reconstruction, the economy and ultimately the system's survival, diplomacy could move forward.

If hardliners succeed in presenting any compromise as surrender, even the indirect talks could collapse.

Based on the positions outlined by both analysts, further reports of progress are likely to be accompanied by contradictory public statements.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: AfD threatens to cut funding for 'modern-thinking' culture
entries.summary: The far-right party could win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September. Their cultural program denigrates Bauhaus, Holocaust remembrance culture and diversity in theater.
entries.content:
August 6, 2026

The far-right party could win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September. Their cultural program denigrates Bauhaus, Holocaust remembrance culture and diversity in theater.

In upcoming state elections to be held on September 6, polls suggest the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could win an absolute majority in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Based on the far-right's cultural policy program, museums, theaters and cultural institutions in the region say that artistic freedom is one of the far-right party's targets.

The AfD has announced that artists and institutions would be required to sign a declaration pledging "not to hold in contempt Germany and its culture" if they want to obtain state funding. Many of these organizations and individuals heavily rely on these subsidies.

The AfD's interpretation of disrespect to German culture also ambiguously includes what the party calls "anti-German art."

"We declared in our government program that we no longer intend to spend public funds on promoting anti-German art," said Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, cultural policy spokesperson for the AfD parliamentary group in the state legislature, in a speech held in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament in late June.

Asked by other members of parliament to specify what that meant exactly, Tillschneider said, "Anti-German art is German art that doesn't want to be German." He mentioned as an example an opera production he had seen some years ago; the classical German composer's work was revisited through a "feminist deconstructivist" lens that didn't please him and corresponds to what he sees as "anti-German art."

"This anti-German aversion is still considered de rigueur in large parts of the theater world," he said. "We will no longer support this attitude — let me state that quite clearly."

Bauhaus, a direct target — like in the 1930s

Bauhaus, Germany's iconic architecture, art and design school founded in 1919, was forced to close under the Nazis, who considered their avant-garde ideas and their open-minded attitude to be "un-German." Bauhaus nevertheless went on to become one of design's most important movements of the 20th century; its influence is still felt worldwide. 

Today, the AfD once again sees Bauhaus as too modernist and globalist for the "patriotic cultural policy" the party envisions.

"The AfD's criticism of Bauhaus picks up on criticism from 100 years ago; their wording is similar," Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Foundation, told DW.

The AfD Saxony-Anhalt's program describes Bauhaus as "a controversial school of architecture" and criticizes the current state government for putting too much emphasis on this landmark attraction in their current image campaign, titled "moderndenken" (thinking modern).

The AfD aims to adopt instead a campaign called "deutschdenken" (thinking German), which would downplay the role of Bauhaus and instead "highlight the state's significant contributions to the development of the German nation — from Henry I and Otto I to Luther, Bismarck and Nietzsche."

Historically loaded language

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) strongly rejects comparisons to the Nazi party and Adolf Hitler, often dismissing them as trivializations of Nazi crimes.

Yet in its cultural policy program, the far-right party regularly adopts the language used in Hitler's propaganda, downplays Nazi-era atrocities, challenges Germany's culture of remembrance and uses historically loaded language.

The proposed "deutschdenken" slogan is one example of this: "'Deutsch denken' refers to a speech Adolf Hitler made in 1938" — the "Reichenberger Rede," noted Steiner.

Culture needs state support to thrive

The Bauhaus is not the only cultural organization that feels threatened in Saxony-Anhalt. "As cultural practitioners, cultural initiators and artists, we can say that we are now genuinely afraid, because what's being triggered there is, in fact, the idea that art and culture must be 'German,'" Annegret Laabs, director of the Kunstmuseum Magdeburg told DW.

Laabs is a spokesperson for the initiative Kultur ist Vielfalt und Heimat, which roughly translates as "Culture is diversity and home." The initiative brings together a wide range of cultural institutions and artists from the region; they are warning in a joint statement that the AfD's plans could have far-reaching consequences for artistic freedom, historical memory, and public cultural life.

"We all know that what we do — from theaters to museums to libraries — is paid for with taxpayer money. It wouldn't exist otherwise," said Laabs.

Restricting funding based on an arbitrary definition of what constitutes "German" art basically equates to culture's demise, explains Laabs: "If we look at the bigger picture, we see that culture and art have been free for centuries and have known no boundaries — not even national ones. Wherever there are national boundaries, there is no longer any art or culture worthy of that name."

'Resist the beginnings'

Along with threats to funding, the AfD's program also describes Germany's existing culture of Holocaust remembrance as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" that has "blocked the possibilities for forming a stable national identity." It sees this as an "identity disorder" that needs to be "healed," by focusing on the "positive aspects of German history."

Sabine Schramm, director of Magdeburg's puppet theater, finds "it regrettable that we humans are not willing to draw conclusions from a complex history — conclusions that matter both to us as individuals and to us as a society."

She notes that throughout her 30-year career in theater, she has dealt with Germany's culture of remembrance, grappling with the horrors of Nazism on stage.

"It has always been important to me — especially in productions for young people — to tell stories that address precisely this issue: National Socialism, how it begins, and how the various elements interlock," she points out.

"I can still see myself standing on stage talking about 'resisting the beginnings' — that phrase, 'resisting the beginnings,' has become such a cliché," she says, referring to an idea Germans are deeply familiar with; after the horrors of the Nazi era, the generations that followed were urged to speak out against threats to democracy — before it's too late.

"But where, exactly, are the beginnings?" Schramm asks. "Is this the beginning, or are we still before the beginning? Are we right in the middle of it? What must I do to resist the beginnings?"

Edited by: Brenda Haas

entries.title: Germany: Leipzig airport drone attack sets off alarm bells
entries.summary: German authorities have begun a counterterrorism ⁠investigation into a drone laden with explosives found near a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport. It is seen as a "hybrid attack scenario."
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Leipzig airport drone attack sets off alarm bells

August 6, 2026

German authorities have begun a counterterrorism ⁠investigation into a drone laden with explosives found near a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport. It is seen as a "hybrid attack scenario."

German airports have seen hundreds of drone alerts, but this incident eclipses them all: in the middle of the night on Wednesday, airport staff at the Leipzig/Halle Airport in the eastern state of Saxony found a drone rigged with explosives on the runway.

Federal police specialists were able to defuse it using a bomb disposal robot. The incident prompted the closure of part of one of Europe's largest cargo hubs.

German media reports say that experts from Saxony state police found the package to contain the highly explosive substances PETN and Semtex, which are also used in military applications. The detonator attached to the package had apparently broken off, which prevented an explosion.

A hybrid threat scenario

This unconfirmed information is particularly significant because the drone was found next to a plane of the Ukrainian state-owned carrier Antonov Airlines. The aircraft was reportedly loaded with military munitions that — according to reports — had just been transported from France to Leipzig and were slated for onward shipment to Ukraine.

Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt cut his vacation short to assess the situation firsthand at the scene. His initial assessment: "This represents a new threat scenario." At a press conference on Wednesday evening, he spoke only in general and vague terms regarding potential perpetrators and motives. However, Dobrindt did not rule out the possibility that "foreign powers" might be behind the incident — with the aim of unsettling Germany.

"All the speculation that is currently going on about the explosives, the construction, the question of the drone, the origin and, of course, who is behind it, is now part of the investigation," Dobrindt said.

In June, Dobrindt created a so-called Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats, as Germany has been on high alert for espionage, sabotage and disinformation, particularly from Russia.

Suspecting links to Russia

Leipzig/Halle Airport is high on the priority list regarding security and, like other airports, is being equipped with technology to detect and intercept drones. At the same time, however, Dobrindt acknowledged that this is an ongoing race: "When drones are designed to bypass technology, the technology itself must be continuously upgraded," he said.

After Frankfurt am Main, Leipzig/Halle Airport is Germany's largest cargo hub. Security experts say this makes it a potential target for state-sponsored attacks. Consequently, counter-terrorism expert Hans-Jakob Schindler considers it possible that Russia could be the mastermind behind the explosive-laden drone.

For the moment, the facts remain unknown. "But given the location — where we have already seen similar disruptions that could be traced back to Russia — that would be my initial assumption," Schindler told DW.

Hybrid attacks generally refer to covert operations that do not aim for direct confrontation, but are designed to create uncertainty. These can involve a combination of various tactics such as sabotage, economic pressure, or disinformation.

Earlier on Thursday, Saxony's Interior Minister Armin Schuster said that authorities are searching for parts of a possible second drone that collided with an aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport.

Germany's anti-drone defense in the spotlight

Drone sightings have frequently disrupted German airports, canceling flights and causing headaches for travelers. Drones are also sometimes sighted over German military installations.

In December last year, Holger Münch, the head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), said that over 1,000 suspicious drones had been registered in 2025, which he said represented a "significant situation of danger."

Leipzig had already been the site of an attempted attack in July 2024: a container belonging to the logistics company DHL caught fire in the airport's cargo area. The cause was a package sent from the Baltic states containing an incendiary device designed — according to investigators — to detonate mid-air. At the time, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office suspected a targeted act of Russian sabotage.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Marine One: Helicopter carrying Trump flew close to passenger jet, FAA plans probe
entries.summary: Trump's helicopter and a passenger jet briefly were too close near Reagan National Airport, prompting an inquiry into what happened to the safety rules adopted after last year's deadly collision.
entries.content:
United States of America

FAA probes Marine One flight close to passenger jet

August 6, 2026

Trump's helicopter and a passenger jet briefly were too close near Reagan National Airport, prompting an inquiry into what happened to the safety rules adopted after last year's deadly collision.

The United States Federal Aviation Administration on Wednesday said it is investigating why a passenger jet was allowed to take off from Reagan Washington National Airport just as President Donald Trump's helicopter, Marine One, was approaching on Tuesday afternoon, in an apparent breach of safety rules adopted after last year's deadly midair collision near the airport.

In January 2025, a collision between an American Airlines jet and an Army helicopter near Reagan National killed 67 people and led to tighter separation rules and radar-based tracking requirements.

What do we know?

Marine One lifted off from near the White House around 2:33 p.m. local time, headed to Joint Base Andrews ahead of a trip to Los Angeles. Reuters cited a source saying the jet involved was Envoy Air Flight 3742, an American Airlines regional jet bound for Pensacola, Florida, which departed a minute later. A second flight, Republic 4700, was rerouted as a precaution after coming within three miles (about 4.8 kilometers) of the airport.

The jet was climbing above Marine One, so the two were never on a collision course.

"Based on our preliminary safety review, there was momentary loss of separation after which the ​aircraft continued to move away from one another," the FAA said on Wednesday. FAA rules require aircraft near airports to stay at least 1.5 miles apart horizontally and 500 feet apart vertically. Both aircraft landed safely.

White House says president was not in danger

"Marine One flights are piloted by some of the best aviators in the world, and at no point was the President in harm's way," White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement.

The Marine Corps defended the helicopter pilots' actions. "There were no 'close calls' with the routine Marine One movement," Marine Corps spokesperson Capt. Jacob Sugg said in an email to the Associated Press.

Under rules adopted after last year's crash, Reagan National is supposed to pause takeoffs and landings whenever a helicopter is on a conflicting route. But sources told Reuters controllers did not halt commercial flights on Tuesday as required. The National Transportation Safety Board said it would investigate, and the FAA said it plans to convene its own safety review.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: How Gianni Infantino rose to rule football
entries.summary: Gianni Infantino is staying on as FIFA president despite growing pressure to step down. So who is football's most powerful man, why did UEFA and others turn against him, and how did he reassert his authority?
entries.content:
Switzerland

How Gianni Infantino rose to rule football

August 6, 2026

Gianni Infantino is staying on as FIFA president despite growing pressure to step down. So who is football's most powerful man, why did UEFA and others turn against him, and how did he reassert his authority?

Despite strong pressure for him to resign, particularly from UEFA, Gianni Infantino convinced FIFA's Board of Management to express their full support for him following a crisis meeting in Rabat on Wednesday. It was the latest development in a crisis that began with news last week of a FIFA plan to create a subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the men's World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20% to be offered to external investors.

Where did Gianni Infantino come from?

Giovanni Vincenzo Infantino was born on March 23, 1970, in the southwestern Swiss town of Brig to Italian parents. Many years later, as FIFA president, he would speak of the discrimination he said he experienced as he grew up for being of Italian heritage in Switzerland. Infantino studied law at the University of Fribourg, before becoming the general secretary of the International Centre for Sports Studies at the University of Neuchatel in 1997. 

What did Infantino do before FIFA?

Infantino, who speaks six languages, first gained notoriety beyond Switzerland after joining UEFA, football's European governing body, in 2000. There, he would climb the corporate ladder to become the organization's general secretary in 2009. Serving under former UEFA President Michel Platini, Infantino's position kept him largely out of the public eye, but during this time his face became a familiar one to European football fans, as one of his roles was hosting the Champions League and Euros draws, broadcast live on TV. 

How did Infantino become FIFA president?

The door to the FIFA presidency was knocked open by the 2015 FIFA corruption scandal in which several officials were indicted, seven of whom were arrested at a Zurich hotel. This came just ahead of a FIFA Congress to elect a new president. Although Sepp Blatter won reelection for a fifth term, he announced his resignation just days later. An extraordinary FIFA Congress was called for February 2016.

Infantino looked a rank outsider when he threw his hat into the ring. Platini, his boss at UEFA, was the favorite, but he withdrew his candidacy a month before the election, after both he and Blatter had been banned over ethics violations involving a dubious payment.

In the days leading up to the vote, Sheik Salman bin Ibrahim al Khalifa of Bahrain emerged as the frontrunner among the seven candidates. However, Infantino, running on a pledge to clean up what was a scandal-ridden organization, won the presidency in the second round of voting. He'd also promised to increase FIFA payments to every member association.

"We will restore the image of FIFA and the respect of FIFA, and everyone in the world will applaud us and will applaud all of you for what we'll do in FIFA in the future," Infantino told the delegates in Zurich's Hallenstadion.

What has Infantino done in power?

Gianni Infantino has presided over a decade of unprecedented growth in revenue for FIFA, culminating in the 2026 World Cup – the first to feature 48 teams and 104 games – compared to 32 teams and 64 games in Qatar four years earlier. This was bound to generate higher revenue, but it was compounded by the dynamic pricing system FIFA introduced for the tournament. This led to sky-high prices for tickets – and FIFA went one better by getting into the secondary market – and taking a 15% cut from both buyer and seller on every transaction. 

While the final revenue numbers won't be announced until FIFA publishes its annual report for 2026, the figures are expected to smash the almost $5.8 billion (€5.03) the organization earned in 2022, largely from the Qatar World Cup. Infantino has spoken of a figure around double that. Others believe it could be far higher.

What controversies has he been involved in?

He says he wasn't to blame for a major talking point at the World Cup – the suspension of USA forward Folarin Balogun's red-card ban following his sending off against Bosnia in the round of 32. This followed a call by US President Donald Trump to Infantino to request a "review." Infantino insisted that an independent FIFA body had made the decision.

The hydration breaks, which effectively split games into four quarters, also didn't go over well with many football fans. Others were angry at his refusal to step in on rows over visas for traveling fans, officials and a referee from Somalia and the treatment of the Iran team in the US during the tournament.

Prior to the World Cup 2026, Infantino had made the headlines for the wrong reasons on several occasions. Among his more notable controversies were:

  • Ahead of the 2017 FIFA Congress in Bahrain, Infantino removed the chairmen of the Ethics Committee, Hans-Joachim Eckert and Cornel Borbely, without giving reasons.
  • A year later he agreed in principle to a deal that would have seen a financial consortium from the Middle East and Asia acquire the rights to the Club World Cup and a global Nations League for a reported $25 billion. The deal never happened.
  • In July 2020, the Swiss public prosecutor's office accused Infantino of inciting abuse of office by meeting secretly with the head of the Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland, Michael Lauber. Three years later the case was dropped due to a lack of evidence.
  • In a truly cringeworthy ceremony at the World Cup draw in December 2025, Infantino presented US President Donald Trump with the newly created FIFA Peace Prize. This could be seen as the culmination of a widely criticized "bromance" between the FIFA boss and Trump.  

Why has Infantino been under such intense pressure to resign?

His problems began with the World Cup sell-off plan. UEFA sharply condemned the news within minutes – before threatening to boycott all FIFA events, including the men's and women's World Cups. After Infantino backed off the plan, UEFA doubled down, saying it had lost confidence in the "current FIFA leadership" and the "task of rebuilding trust in FIFA" had just begun. Football's European governing body also threatened action through its US lawyers over what it termed a "shabby, backroom, opaque deal."

How did he reassert himself?

The FIFA boss summoned senior staff members to an emergency meeting in Rabat on Wednesday. A statement issued after that meeting conceded that "mistakes made were acknowledged" in connection with the private investment plan and that the "process should have been handled differently."

It also said those present had "reaffirmed their full support" for the president and stressed that FIFA would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation."

Edited by: Matt Pearson

entries.title: Africa and the ICC: Why most countries are staying
entries.summary: A new wave of African withdrawals has swept through the International Criminal Court. Chad turned its back on the court after three junta-led states in the Sahel exited. But most African countries still trust The Hague.
entries.content:
August 6, 2026

A new wave of African withdrawals has swept through the International Criminal Court. Chad turned its back on the court after three junta-led states in the Sahel exited. But most African countries still trust The Hague.

The establishment of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2002 was seen as a breakthrough in the global fight against war crimes, genocide, and crimes against humanity.

Yet criticism from parts of Africa is almost as old as the ICC itself: Time and again, the court has been accused of targeting Africa in a one-sided manner. Recently, this criticism has grown louder again — and culminated in a veritable wave of withdrawals.

At the end of July, Chad also announced its withdrawal from the court in The Hague: The government stated that the ICC's effectiveness was "limited and unbalanced."

In September 2025, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger initiated their withdrawal from the ICC, accusing it of being a neocolonialist tool of the West. The withdrawals officially take effect one year after they are announced.

At the same time, the ICC is at the center of a scandal: Its members have voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct. Khan has denied wrongdoing.

Justice: Withdrawal or accountability?

The wave of withdrawals from the ICC is cause for concern, says Attila Kisla, head of the International Justice Group at the Southern Africa Litigation Centre in Johannesburg. Especially since some of these countries cited an alleged bias against Africa among the reasons.

"It is important to remember, however, that many of the proceedings — particularly in the early stages — were based on voluntary referrals by African countries seeking the court's assistance,” Kisla told DW.

In 1998, Senegal became the first country to sign the Rome Statute, the international treaty that established the ICC in 2002. Today, 125 countries are parties to the statute. Of these, 33 are African states, representing about 60% of the continent.

The ICC aims to prosecute the most serious crimes under international law and operates according to the so-called principle of complementarity: It can only take action when states are unwilling or unable to prosecute certain crimes themselves.

However, according to Kisla, the fact that there have been no significant proceedings against individuals from powerful states or Western countries has not helped the court's image.

The US itself is not a member of the court but its citizens could be prosecuted if they are accused of crimes committed on the territory of member states.

Furthermore, one must not ignore the current global political climate: "These withdrawals are taking place at a time when the US has openly declared its intention to dissolve the ICC and is exerting unprecedented pressure on the court and its supporters,” said Kisla. 

The ICC has also issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Benjamin Netanyahu, even though neither Russia nor Israel is a state party.

In these politically charged times, the large number of African states that remain parties to the Rome Statute is of crucial importance: "Their continued membership reflects a conscious decision to defend international justice at a time when the ICC is under political attack,” said Kisla.

Conversely, however, according to Kisla, every decision to remain in the ICC also sends an important message: "Accountability for atrocities must not depend on politics or power,” he told DW. "It reflects a commitment to the rule of law and ensures that victims and survivors continue to have access to justice when domestic systems fail."

War crimes victims lose protection

For the human rights organization Amnesty International (AI), the withdrawal of the four Sahel region states is a setback for the right to justice of the people in the affected countries.

"As victims of war crimes, genocide, and crimes against humanity, they are losing their last resort when they cannot find justice in their own countries," said Alice Banens, a legal expert at AI's regional office for West and Central Africa in Dakar.

She, too, describes these withdrawals as "attacks on the integrity of the international system and the International Criminal Court.” These fit into the broader context in which the ICC is facing attacks and sanctions from several states aimed at weakening the court's ability to fulfill its mandate.

Amnesty has called on the states that have withdrawn so far — Burundi was the first African state to do so in 2016 — to voice any criticism within the system through discussions in the Assembly of State Parties to the Rome Statute.

Former member states can also reverse their decision: For example, South Africa formally initiated its withdrawal from the ICC in 2016 but halted the process in March 2017. The occasion was the state visit of Sudan's then President Omar al-Bashir, against whom the court had issued an arrest warrant for war crimes in Darfur. The South African government refused to arrest him.

More prosecutions outside Africa

According to Banens, there is still a widespread perception today that African issues dominate the ICC's agenda. "That is simply not true,” she told DW. "While this was the case in the early years of the ICC's work — when most, if not all, investigations concerned the situation in Africa.”

Today, however, more active investigations are taking place outside Africa than within the continent — for example, in Afghanistan, the Palestinian territories, Venezuela, the Philippines, and Ukraine, according to Banens.

Some states considering withdrawal argue that the ICC interferes with domestic legal processes and national reconciliation, according to Christopher Isike, a professor of international relations at the University of Pretoria.

"African countries, as well as major powers such as the US, Russia, and China — which are not members and do not recognize the ICC's jurisdiction—have also cited this as a reason for their criticism," Isike told DW.

Nevertheless, according to Isike, the ICC provides an external mechanism for accountability when countries recognize that their domestic judicial systems lack the independence or the political will to prosecute political or military officials.

According to Isike, countries such as Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and even Mali have in the past themselves requested the ICC's intervention because they lack the capacity to prosecute the perpetrators. This weakens the argument that any intervention by the court constitutes outside interference. "This perception of selective justice is the main reason for this way of thinking.”

There are also governments for which remaining a member of the ICC signals their commitment to human rights, democratic governance, and international law, according to Isike: "They believe that this gives them diplomatic credibility as a form of soft power,” he said.

For Isike, the debate over inequality in the justice system touches on something fundamental: the competition for the international order. African governments do not, in principle, reject international justice. "They want a system that is more universal and uniform and gives less cause for accusations of political selectivity.”

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

entries.title: Munich car-ramming attacker sentenced to life in prison
entries.summary: A Munich court has handed down the toughest possible sentence over the 2025 attack that killed a mother and her toddler and injured dozens more.
entries.content:
August 6, 2026

A Munich court has handed down the toughest possible sentence over the 2025 attack that killed a mother and her toddler and injured dozens more.

A German court has sentenced Farhad N. to life in prison for murder and attempted murder over a deadly car attack on a Verdi trade union demonstration in Munich.

A 37-year-old mother and her two-year-old child were killed in the February 2025 attack, while more than 40 people were injured.

What did the court decide about the Munich attack

The Higher Regional Court in the Bavarian capital also found that the 25-year-old Afghan national bore a particularly serious degree of guilt, making an early release less likely.

The court found that N. deliberately drove into the demonstration from behind.

Presiding judge Michael Höhne described the scene as "a scene of devastation" stretching 12 meters (about 40 feet) across and 23 meters long.

The court convicted N. of two counts of murder and 23 counts of attempted murder, one more attempted murder count than federal prosecutors had sought.

He was also convicted of 19 counts of dangerous bodily harm and three counts of intentional bodily harm.

The sentence matched the demand from federal prosecutors.

The defense had called for a 15-year prison term and for N. to be placed in psychiatric care.

Prosecutors said the attack appeared to have been driven by a complex mix of motives, including religious and political factors, loneliness and diffuse fears.

N. did not explain his motive during the trial.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and obliges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

entries.title: Germany: 10 years of 'Integration Act' for refugees
entries.summary: The German Integration Act aimed to regulate the integration of recognized refugees following high levels of immigration, facilitating access to the labor market in return for integration efforts.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: 10 years of 'Integration Act' for refugees

August 6, 2026

The German Integration Act aimed to regulate the integration of recognized refugees following high levels of immigration, facilitating access to the labor market in return for integration efforts.

In early August 2016, a phrase began circulating in Germany that would shape political and societal discussions for many years to come: "the divided society."

There were still many Germans who remained committed to welcoming hundreds of thousands of refugees who had begun arriving the previous year, mainly from Syria. However, an increasing number were more skeptical of immigrants and foreigners, especially following the mass sexual assaults involving young men with immigrant backgrounds that took place in Cologne on New Year's Eve 2015–2016.

Under the leadership of Chancellor Angela Merkel, the coalition government of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) sought to calm the polarized mood in Germany by introducing an integration act , a law designed to appeal to all sides through the guiding principle of "support and challenge" ("fördern und fordern").

Some thought it offered too many giveaways; others felt it imposed too many demands.

'Support and challenge' means squaring the circle

"For someone in favor of strong regulatory policy, the integration law offered too much assistance while demanding far too little. One example is the fact that a rejected asylum application did not necessarily lead to deportation," says Holger Kolb, of the Expert Council on Integration and Migration (SVR).

"For someone very concerned with integration policy, on the other hand, the requirements were far too high, especially regarding temporary residence permits for vocational training. They believe this creates far too many obstacles to successful integration."

Providing support for new arrivals meant massively expanding integration and language courses, allowing new arrivals to enter the labor market more quickly. A vocational training permit for refugees whose individual asylum applications had been rejected, but whose home countries were still categorized as unsafe, allowed them to complete a three-year vocational training program followed by two years of employment in the field they trained in.

On the other hand, it was made obligatory to participate in language and integration courses. Sanctions were imposed in the form of welfare benefit cuts for those who refused to participate. Also, the refugees were distributed evenly across Germany to prevent over-concentration in major cities.

Criticisms of the residence requirement

This "residency requirement" had a very negative impact on integration, says Herbert Brücker, head of the Research Department for Migration, Integration and International Labour Studies at the Institute for Employment Research (IAB).

"People were distributed disproportionately to economically weak regions with high unemployment. If we restrict people to regions where the economy isn't doing so well, that naturally has negative effects on labor market integration," Brücker explained.

However, he has a positive assessment of the vocational training policy, which allowed rejected refugees to finish their vocational training. He argues that it always makes sense to offer those who integrate well the prospect of staying: They put more effort into learning the language and finding employment and ultimately contribute to the social security systems.

Integration in Germany is better than many think

And it turns out, integration in Germany isn't going nearly as badly as has often been claimed, says Brücker, even if refugees are entering the labor market much more slowly than other immigrants.

"Ten years later, we're now seeing employment rates of 65% to 67% — just 3% below the national average. This puts Germany at the top of the European rankings, alongside Norway. This is also due to the fact that we've offered integration courses, language programs and vocational training to actively promote integration."

The Federal Ministry of the Interior and the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) has partially scrapped plans to severely restrict free access to integration courses to only those with "good prospects of remaining in the country." Since June 2026, Ukrainians and EU citizens have once again been able to participate in the courses — including those without a secure prospect of remaining.

Brücker points out that integration courses are a relatively inexpensive tool for integration. "They increase employment rates by five to ten percentage points once people complete the course. Cutting funding for integration courses delays integration into the labor market and prolongs reliance on benefits. This doesn't save money — it actually costs us a lot of money."

Room for improvement

Were Brücker able to refine the Integration Act, he says he would relax the residency requirement after asylum proceedings are concluded, begin integration courses just one month after arrival and expedite asylum proceedings in order to integrate people with protection status more quickly while also being able to deport those without protection status more quickly.

Kolb, however, wants to see more coordination between the federal government and the states, and a simpler regulatory framework.

The Integration Act of August 2016, he says, does not really deserve that name. "People expect the Integration Act to provide comprehensive regulations governing the integration of people who are already here," he says.

"In reality, however, the Integration Act is specifically designed for people who have come here as refugees. It would have made more sense to manage expectations better, and establish regulations that are significantly simpler."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Middle East: Hormuz deal near, IDF soldiers dead in Lebanon
entries.summary: Iran has said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is in its "final stage" if the US doesn't obstruct it. Two Israeli soldiers were killed in southern Lebanon. Follow DW for the latest.
entries.content:
Middle East

Middle East: Hormuz deal near, IDF soldiers dead in Lebanon

Published August 6, 2026last updated August 6, 2026

Iran has said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is in its "final stage" if the US doesn't obstruct it. Two Israeli soldiers were killed in southern Lebanon. Follow DW for the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Iran's Foreign Ministry says a deal with Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz will come very soon 'if certain parties do not obstruct this process'

  • Pakistan has praised Oman for work 'resolving the Hormuz issue'

  • Amid renewed strikes on southern Lebanon, Israel says two of its soldiers were killed Thursday

  • Oman faces an environmental disaster after explosions rocked a Russian oil tanker in its waters

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about the Middle East on Thursday, August 6:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Houthis kill dozens of Yemeni forces, officials say

Houthis kill dozens of Yemeni forces, officials say

Attacks by the Houthi militant group in Yemen have killed at least 30 government soldiers and wounded at least 50 more, Yemeni government officials said.

The attacks hit the provinces of Marib and Hadhramaut.

A missile hit troops during their morning formation at a camp in Marib province, "killing and wounding at least 45 personnel," an official, who declined to be named for security reasons, to the AFP news agency.

The Houthis did not immediately comment on the attacks.

The Houthis have been at war with the Yemeni government since 2014. The conflict has killed hundreds of thousands of people and set off a humanitarian crisis in Yemen.

Skip next section Pakistan praises Oman, hopes Strait of Hormuz agreement can lead to peace

Pakistan praises Oman, hopes Strait of Hormuz agreement can lead to peace

Pakistan, which has mediated talks with Oman and Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz, said Oman played an important role in "resolving the Hormuz issue."

Further, Islamabad's Foreign Ministry expressed hope that a new deal between Muscat and Tehran could also open the door to peace talks between Iran and the United States.

"We hope that the agreement on the strait will pave the way for continuing dialog, particularly the resumption of technical level talks between Iran and the United States," said a Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman on Thursday.

Skip next section Oil tanker reports explosions in Strait of Hormuz

Oil tanker reports explosions in Strait of Hormuz

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) on Thursday posted on X that the captain of an oil tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz had reported hearing two explosions. The post noted that no crew members had been harmed in the incident, nor had any damage been caused.

The explosions were registered early Thursday, while the ship was cruising about 9 nautical miles (17 kilometers) southeast of Kumzar, Oman.

Separately, Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed to have struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea — the eighth and ninth Saudi vessels targeted by the group since it announced a blockade of Saudi oil as part of the broader conflict arising from the Iran war.

A spokesman for the militant group claimed Houthi fighters had hit one tanker, the Wafa, in the Red Sea; and another, the Daisy, in the Gulf of Aden.

Skip next section Oil spill from suspected Russian tanker off Oman has doubled in size

Oil spill from suspected Russian tanker off Oman has doubled in size

The amount of oil escaping from a suspected Russian shadow fleet tanker has increased greatly in recent days, observers say.

The Caroline Bezengi, an internationally sanctioned Russian vessel transporting 1 million barrels of illicit oil, reported two explosions of unknown cause in June and has been stranded since.

Satellite imagery shows the slick of oil escaping into the protected waters of the Arabian Sea Reserve growing to cover an estimated 90-kilometer-long (56-mile) stretch — twice that of a week ago — near al-Qibliyyah island, off Oman's southern coast.

Russia's shadow fleet consists of older vessels, often in poor condition, that are flagged variously and sell Moscow's oil to pay for President Vladimir Putin's now four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine.

Speaking to the state of such vessels and their ultimate aim, Greenpeace Germany on Thursday said, "This dramatic expansion (of the oil spill) underscores the serious and continuing environmental threat posed by the stranded tanker — and exemplifies the dangers associated with the practices of Russia's shadow fleet."

The Caroline Bezengi was reported to have loaded its cargo in the Russian Black Sea port of Sheskharis on May 11.

Explosions were reported on the ship on June 6.

Its last radio signal was transmitted on June 11, when it was off the coast of Yemen.

It is estimated that the vessel became stranded at its present position between June 18 and 23.

Skip next section IDF soldiers killed in southern Lebanon operations

IDF soldiers killed in southern Lebanon operations

Israel on Thursday said that two of its soldiers were killed during operations in southern Lebanon when an improvised explosive device detonated during a house search. Four more soldiers were seriously injured in the blast.

The incident occurred near the Lebanese village of Majdal Zoun.

Previously, Israel pounded southern Lebanon with bombs on Wednesday in response to what it said was a "blatant violation" of a June ceasefire agreement by the Iran-backed militia Hezbollah.

Lebanon’s Health Ministry said one person had been killed and 12 injured in the Israeli strikes.

Under the terms of the ceasefire agreement, the Lebanese army is tasked with disarming Hezbollah, which operates independently of the government, and Israel is supposed to withdraw its troops from Lebanese territory.

Currently, Israeli and Lebanese diplomats are trying to put together a longer-term peace agreement at negotiations being held in Rome, Italy.

Skip next section Iran says Hormuz deal in 'final stage'

Iran says Hormuz deal in 'final stage'

Iran's Foreign Ministry on Thursday said that a deal with Oman regarding control over the Strait of Hormuz is in its "final stage" and will soon be in place "if certain parties do not obstruct this process."

Though not mentioned by name, the inference is that US President Donald Trump — who triggered the shutdown of the all-important waterway when he launched his war with Iran on February 28 — will again scupper a return to shipping flow.  

"The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," Iran's Foreign Ministry said.

Mediator Pakistan praised Oman's role in making the Tehran-Muscat deal a reality, adding that it would pave the way for comprehensive peace negotiations between Iran and the US.

The strait agreement could see ships traveling through Iranian and Omani waters and paying fees for safe passage.

Iran has insisted that it will exert control over the international passageway — through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas supply generally flows — but the US has insisted traffic must flow freely and without fees, as it did before Trump ordered US attacks on Iran.

Currently, the US has a blockade on the blockade, with Iran controlling the movement of ships through the narrow passage and the US maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

As the world economy sputters under the increased economic strain brought on by the US war, Trump has faced growing pressure from his Republican underlings in Congress to end the unpopular, price-busting conflict before November's mid-term elections.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from DW's Bonn newsroom and our coverage of today's events in the Middle East.

There are new developments in the on again, off again saga over whether the Strait of Hormuz — one of the world's most crucial international shipping passages — will ever be reopened; and if so, how, with Iran announcing that a deal is in its "final stages."

Tehran warned against "obstruction," however, hinting that the US could blow up the deal between Iran and Oman for control of the strait.

Pakistan, which mediated negotiations between Tehran and Muscat, praised Oman for getting the agreement done. Now Muscat can focus some of its attention on a suspected Russian shadow-fleet tanker that is leaking massive amounts of oil into its waters after two explosions rocked the vessel.

Israel on Thursday reported that two of its soldiers were killed and four injured in operations in southern Lebanon, where its forces continue to hunt members of the Iran-backed militant Islamist group Hezbollah.

Stay tuned to DW for the latest Middle East news here.
